In that file there's a typo in which sigma[g,d] was commented out. Fixed in this attachment.

You don't need to explicitly specify uniform priors. But, if you intend to use a uniform(0,100) prior, you should restrict the upper bound of sigma as well, with:

vector<lower=0,upper=100>[D] sigma[G];

Another potential problem is p failing to be in the (0,1) interval. You might try declaring p at the top of the model {} block and doing something like

  for (n in 1:N) {
    p <- gamma + (1 - gamma) * Phi(x[n] * beta[ss[n]]);
    p <- if_else(step(1.0 - p), p, 0.99999);
    y[n] ~ bernoulli(p); # fitting as a cumulative normal (probit) model.
  }

Although if that step() ever binds after the warmup phase, then there are modeling issues.

Looks like Ben's and my comments crossed again, so some
of this is redundant.

On 12/11/12 5:16 PM, Tom Wallis wrote:
> In that file there's a typo in which sigma[g,d] was commented out. Fixed in this attachment.

One issue is that you have:

sigma[g,d] ~ uniform(0,100);

but declare sigma as:

vector<lower=0>[D] sigma[G]; # population level standard deviation on the beta weights.

What you want is to declare sigma with a constraint
that matches the support of its sampling distribution, i.e.,
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[D] sigma[G];

With the constraint in place, the sampling statement
isn't even needed, as the constraint places a uniform
distribution on sigma over its support [0,100]. You can
include it for clarity -- the Stan compiler is smart enough to
simply eliminate the unnecessary computation (we can
figure out which parts of a probability function are needed up
to a constant based on the parameter vs. data declarations).

It turns out that I ran the .Rdata file without
knowing it after I downloaded everything. So much for
computer safety!

It looks to me like your model runs with

stan(..., init=0, ...)

and I've appended the output below. The traceplot for lp__
(the total log probability) show that the zero inits are
not very good in an lp__ sense, but Stan converges to the
region of the solution within 50 or so iterations. (I've attached
the traceplot for lp__.)

With random inits, it can't find a good initial step size.
Our very diffuse default inits can be a problem in regression settings.

You can make things much faster by vectorizing, as in
replacing

for (s in 1:S) e_beta[s] ~ normal(0,1);

with

e_beta ~ normal(0,1);

and so on.

You can run into problems with stability with super-broad
priors like the following:

mu[g,d] ~ normal(0,100);

Do you really expect mu values to be in the -300 to 300
range or can you lower the scale from 100 here?

- Bob

parts:
On 12/11/12 6:15 PM, Tom Wallis wrote:
> Dear Bob and Ben,
>
> Thanks for the suggestions. Sorry about the binary file Bob.
>
> 1. I implemented the upper constraint on sigma, a less-crazy prior on mu (100 down to 10 sd) and ran stan with init=0.
> This again crashed, but this time printed out more info from the test gradient (pasted below).

I don't know what the problem is on your side. Did
you try init=0? With that, your original model worked just
fine.

We need to put something in that'll allow variable inits,
but less diffuse than (-2,2) uniform on the unconstrained
scale. (That'll init positive scale parameters in the range
(1/10, 10) and unconstrained parameters on the (-2,2) scale.

Problems arise if the initial state is too far away
from where an actual sample from the posterior would
be.
> 2. I tried to implement the if_else check on the bounds of p suggested by Ben and got

This is an old BUGS trick that you shouldn't need in Stan.
We wrote the robustness into our inv_logit function.

> no matches for function name="if_else"
> arg 0 type=real
> arg 1 type=real
> arg 2 type=real
> expression is ill formed
> Parser expecting: <eps>
>
> p was declared as real at the top of the model block so not sure what's going on there.

The first argument needs to be an int. That's
why Ben was using step(). We're adding general
comparison and boolean operators in the next release,
so this should be easier.

> 3. I did have trouble with stan_rdump. The data that I pass to the stan function in R is a list of the following form:
>
> |
> stanDat <- list(N = nrow(dat),
> y = dat$correct,
> D = ncol(X),
> x = X,
> ss = as.numeric(dat$subject),
> S = length(unique(dat$subject)),
> gg = groupVec,
> G = length(unique(dat$group3)),
> gamma = gamma)
> |
>
>
> I've never used dump so I wasn't too sure what to do, but passing
>
> |
> stan_rdump('stanDat',file='tryDump.Rdump')
The first argument should be a list, not a string.

>
> just gives an empty file called 'tryDump'. Running the example for stan_rdump using
> |
> example(stan_rdump)
> |
>
> pastes the example into the command window but doesn't appear to output any file called "xyz.Rdump". I wasn't then sure


> 4. Thanks for the vectorising tips. I was aware that my code could be vectorised but I attempted to do so today and got
> errors with the multiplication for x[n] * beta[ss[n]] within the cumulative normal statement (could not find function
> "multiply", meaning I suppose that the beta (changed to type matrix) and the row vector x[n] were not conformable).

if x[n] is a ROW vector and beta[ss[n]] is a matrix, then you should
be able to do x[n] * beta[ss[n]]. The error message will tell you
what types it thought you were giving it. Here, beta is
a 2-dimensional structure, so beta[ss[n]] will be a row vector
and you probably don't intend to multiply two row vectors.

> COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'stanModel1' NOW.
> SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'stanModel1' NOW (CHAIN 1).
>
> TEST GRADIENT MODE

You can see the wide range of gradients in your output,
from 3 to 30K. This is very hard to adapt to numerically.
- Bob

> I'm not sure if this is the desired behaviour for that argument (I thought it printed all evaluations?).

It doesn't sample when test_grad is used. We should
remove the error message, because it's not an error,
but rather not trying to sample on purpose.

> In any case, it is the inits that were causing the original error I posted as you suspected. If inits are set to zero
> the model gets through the samples just fine (though I assume in this case I can't really use the Rhat values, since the
> initial values were not diffuse);

You can still use the Rhat values. There's still randomness.
In fact, the very first step will choose momenta that will take
you away from 0 pretty quickly. That's why you'll see lots of
movement in the traceplots and you'll see Rhat values well above
1.

You always have a problem with Rhat that it's only a rejection
test. If Rhat values are not near 1, you know you haven't converged.
But if they're near 1, you don't know that you have converged.

> if inits are set to random then the sampler fails with the error "Initialization
> failed after 100 attempts. Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing
> the model."
>
> Thanks for all your help sorting this out. Any recommendations for how to proceed with these models? Set my own inits?

You can set your own inits based on previous output and then
add some noise. But you'll have to put them back onto the constrained
scale of the model. The auto-init is on the unconstrained (transformed
param) scale.

We're going to add a feature that will add a little noise around
user-specified inits for just this situation.

The root of the problem is that there's only so much arithmetic
precision out there from which to recover. In theory, we'd be fine
if we had arbitrary precision arithmetic (though it might be slow
to converge). But regression problems are really taxing because of
the form of the likelihood, so there's only so much overdispersion in the
inits that remains arithmetically tractable.

- Bob

parts:
On 12/12/12 4:09 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Should we perhaps suggest that examples be sent with preset seeds, to aid replicability? I would prefer fixed seeds than inits=0 as a default!

Even without preset seeds, Stan dumps out the seed as part
of the output to allow replication.

The problem arises when the sampler can't recover from
parameter settings that are too far away from where they
should be.

I'm having this same problem with the model I'm working
on for data annotation, so I take some crude empirical
estimates of some parameters as a starting point.

By fitting with inits=0, you get a feeling for where the
solution is, which will then let you do some inits with
noise around that.

We might also consider lowering the initial dispersion
from [-2,2] to something more modest. That's a pretty
big range for a regression problem with lots of coeffs.

- Bob
